Sparse MoE routing assigns each token to a fixed-size subset of experts (typically top-k by gating score), meaning the router's learned partitioning of input space must generalize from training distribution to inference distribution — and there's no reason to expect it will. The central question is: when the input distribution shifts at inference time, do tokens land on experts that were undertrained on that region of feature space, and how does this compound across layers in a deep MoE stack? Key concepts are router collapse (where shifted inputs concentrate on a small subset of experts, violating load balance), expert specialization brittleness (each expert has learned a narrow function over its training token population, making it poorly calibrated on out-of-distribution tokens it now receives), and the mismatch between the router's confidence in its assignment and the expert's actual competence for that token. What a beginner misses is that the router and the experts are co-adapted during training: the router learned to send tokens to experts that can handle them, but a distribution shift can break this contract silently — the gating scores remain high and confident while the expert is effectively being queried outside its competence envelope, producing no visible error signal. The deeper expert worry is that auxiliary load-balancing losses (importance loss, z-loss) are designed to enforce uniform routing during training, but they actively suppress the routing entropy signal you'd need to detect that inference-time distribution shift has occurred — so the very regularization that stabilizes training conceals distribution shift at deployment.

Each expert in a trained MoE is effectively a low-rank affine map over a compact region of the token embedding manifold — when an OOD token lands on it, the expert produces an output that lies in the span of its training activations but at an extrapolated, often high-magnitude point, since the FFN's SwiGLU or GELU nonlinearities saturate or enter linear regimes outside the training envelope. Geometrically, this looks like a vector with inflated norm and misaligned direction relative to what the residual stream expects to integrate — Zoph et al.'s ST-MoE (2022) observed that expert outputs under distributional pressure could produce logit variance spikes, which they partially addressed with z-loss on router logits, but this treats the symptom (router instability) rather than the expert output geometry problem. The residual stream in a transformer MoE makes this hard to detect because it adds expert outputs additively to a running representation that has already been shaped by attention and previous layers — a single expert's malformed output is diluted by the residual connection, so the Frobenius norm of the corrupted layer output may not spike detectably, especially when only top-1 or top-2 experts fire. In Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2021), the top-1 routing means there's no second expert output to provide a consistency check — if the single selected expert is miscalibrated, there is no ensemble signal to cancel the error, and the next layer's attention mechanism receives a subtly corrupted key/query projection that propagates silently. Critically, layer normalization applied before each subsequent sublayer re-scales the corrupted residual back into a "normal-looking" magnitude range, destroying the norm-based signal that might otherwise flag the anomaly — this is the core detection problem that a beginner, reasoning about norms and distances, entirely misses.

The most promising inference-time signal is router entropy per layer — the Shannon entropy of the softmax gating distribution before top-k truncation — because distribution shift tends to either collapse entropy (tokens confidently routed to a single undertrained expert) or inflate it (the router becomes uncertain, spreading mass across experts that are all poor fits); either deviation from the training-time entropy baseline is a detectable anomaly without any labeled OOD data. A second quantity is expert output cosine variance across the top-k candidates: even if you only execute the top-1 expert, you can cheaply compute the gating scores for top-2 and top-3 and ask whether the score gap (the margin between rank-1 and rank-2) has narrowed relative to training-time statistics — a collapsing margin indicates the router is genuinely uncertain, which is a proxy for the token sitting near an expert boundary in a shifted region of feature space. Third, pre-norm residual stream kurtosis — the fourth moment of the pre-LayerNorm activation distribution across the sequence — is sensitive to the heavy-tailed outputs that OOD expert activations produce before normalization erases them; Dettmers et al.'s LLM.int8() work (2022) identified systematic outlier dimensions in transformer hidden states, and tracking per-dimension kurtosis is cheap and correlates with representational stress. Fourth, cross-layer routing consistency — whether the same token is routed to semantically related experts in consecutive MoE layers — can be checked by maintaining a small routing history buffer; under distribution shift, routing becomes erratic across layers for the same token position in a way that trained models don't exhibit, because deep MoE stacks develop implicit routing curricula (Eigen et al. observed this in hierarchical MoE contexts). The practical obstacle is that all of these require storing per-layer routing statistics from training-time to serve as baselines, which is architecturally straightforward but not implemented in any current production MoE serving stack (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) as of mid-2025 — the gap between what's detectable in principle and what's monitored in practice is almost total.

The cleanest training-time intervention is to replace the standard softmax router with a evidential deep learning formulation — specifically, parameterizing the router to output Dirichlet concentration parameters rather than logits, so that the gating distribution has an explicit epistemic uncertainty estimate (total evidence) separate from the routing decision itself; tokens with low total evidence would trigger a fallback path (a dense expert, a sentinel token, or an abstain signal) rather than confident misrouting. The pathology this creates is immediate: during training on in-distribution data, the model is never rewarded for high uncertainty, so the Dirichlet concentrations collapse toward point masses anyway unless you explicitly inject OOD examples or use a contrastive uncertainty objective — and synthetic OOD data for a general-purpose language model is essentially undefined, which is why evidential approaches have succeeded in vision (Sensoy et al., 2018) but remain largely unapplied to MoE routing. A second architectural approach is stochastic routing with learned temperature annealing, where the router's softmax temperature is conditioned on a running estimate of input novelty (e.g., distance from a prototype bank of training token embeddings maintained via exponential moving average); this makes routing entropy a function of novelty by construction, but introduces a prototype bank that must be updated online — creating catastrophic interference between the prototype update dynamics and the router's optimization, since stale prototypes produce miscalibrated novelty signals. A third option is to train with an explicit routing consistency loss across augmented views of the same token (analogous to self-supervised consistency regularization), penalizing the router for assigning different experts to semantically equivalent inputs — this improves router smoothness at decision boundaries but incentivizes the router to learn coarser partitions of feature space, reducing the expert specialization that makes MoE efficient in the first place. The fundamental pathology across all three approaches is a specialization-robustness tradeoff: the sharp, confident routing that enables expert specialization and parameter efficiency is precisely what makes the router brittle under shift, and any objective that softens routing decisions to gain uncertainty awareness proportionally degrades the sparse activation efficiency that motivated the MoE architecture.

Direct empirical evidence specifically measuring hierarchical MoE robustness under distribution shift is thin, but the closest relevant work is GShard (Lepikhin et al., 2021) and Switch Transformer comparisons against dense models on multilingual translation, where cross-lingual transfer — a natural distribution shift stress test — showed MoE models degrading faster than dense baselines on low-resource languages despite higher average performance, suggesting flat routing is indeed brittle. The theoretical mechanism favoring hierarchical routing is coarse router inertia: a two-level hierarchy where the coarse router partitions by broad semantic/syntactic category (e.g., syntactic structure vs. factual content vs. code) and the fine router handles within-group specialization means a distribution-shifted token is more likely to land in the correct coarse group even if it confuses the fine router — the coarse partition is learned over a larger token population with more statistical support, making it more robust to the long tail of distributional variation. Mixtral 8x7B (Mistral AI, 2024) uses flat top-2 routing across 8 experts, and inspection of its routing patterns (Jiang et al.) showed that the two selected experts are frequently from complementary functional clusters — effectively implementing soft hierarchical behavior emergently, which may partly explain its stronger cross-domain generalization relative to Switch-style top-1 models. The mechanism that would make hierarchy formally beneficial is error containment: in a flat router, a misrouting error immediately selects a miscalibrated leaf expert; in a hierarchy, the coarse router's error must compound with the fine router's error before a fully miscalibrated expert is reached, and if the two routing errors are even weakly negatively correlated (coarse router uncertain → fine router defaults to centroid expert), the joint misrouting probability is lower than either marginal. However, the pathology that undermines this in practice is coarse router ossification: the coarse partition is trained jointly with the fine routers, and the fine routers' specialization creates pressure on the coarse router to maintain stable group boundaries — under distribution shift, this rigidity means the coarse router may confidently assign a shifted token to the wrong group, after which the fine router's within-group specialization provides zero recovery, making the failure worse than flat routing because the error is locked in earlier in the decision tree.

The order of routing decisions matters deeply because it determines which representation is used to make which commitment — in top-down routing, the coarse decision is made from the raw (or shallowly transformed) token embedding before any expert has processed it, whereas in a bottom-up scheme, fine-grained expert affinities would be computed first and the coarse assignment would emerge from their aggregation, meaning the coarse decision is made from a richer, more discriminative representation that has already resolved local ambiguity. No production MoE system implements genuine bottom-up routing, but Mixture of Depths (Raposo et al., 2024) gestures at the relevant intuition: by making the routing decision about whether to apply computation at all contingent on the token's representational state after partial processing, it demonstrates that deferring routing commitments to later in the computational graph improves efficiency and generalization — the same logic applies to hierarchical routing order. The fundamental reason bottom-up aggregation would behave differently under shift is statistical robustness of aggregation: if fine-grained expert affinity scores are computed independently and the coarse assignment is their argmax cluster, then a distribution-shifted token that confuses two fine experts within the correct coarse group produces a noisy but recoverable fine-level signal, whereas the same token in top-down routing gets locked into a wrong coarse group before fine resolution can correct it. However, bottom-up routing creates a severe training instability: the coarse assignment gradient must flow backward through the fine routing decisions, creating a bi-level optimization problem where the coarse router's loss landscape is defined by the fine routers' current state — this is analogous to the instability in neural architecture search with weight sharing (DARTS, Liu et al., 2019), where the architecture parameters and weight parameters interfere destructively during joint optimization. The deeper issue is that bottom-up routing likely destroys load balance by design: fine-grained affinity scores computed independently will naturally cluster — tokens similar at the fine level will aggregate into the same coarse groups, producing exactly the expert collapse and load imbalance that auxiliary losses are designed to prevent, meaning you'd need a load-balancing objective that operates at both levels simultaneously with carefully tuned relative weighting to avoid one level dominating.

The scaling evidence strongly favors increasing expert count over hierarchy depth for raw perplexity: Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2021) showed consistent perplexity gains scaling from 2 to 2048 experts with flat top-1 routing on C4, with diminishing but positive returns throughout, and crucially these gains came without any hierarchical structure — suggesting that flat routing with sufficient experts can approximate any functional decomposition a hierarchy would impose, since the router can learn arbitrary partitions of feature space given enough experts to assign them to. The theoretical argument for flat-over-hierarchy is that a hierarchy imposes an inductive bias about the structure of the token distribution — assuming it decomposes into nested clusters — whereas flat routing with many experts is a more general function approximator that can recover hierarchical structure if it exists without being constrained by it if it doesn't; GLaM (Du et al., 2022) with 64 experts per layer and flat top-2 routing achieved better sample efficiency than dense T5-XXL, and its routing analysis showed emergent functional specialization without any imposed structure. However, the critical confound in all expert-count scaling studies is parameter budget control: adding experts increases total parameters but not active parameters per token, so comparing flat-64-expert against flat-8-expert conflates routing expressivity with raw capacity — the cleaner comparison (same total parameters, different expert granularity) is almost never reported, making it hard to isolate routing structure as the variable. Expert choice routing (Zhou et al., 2022) inverts the standard formulation by having each expert select its top-k tokens rather than each token selecting experts, and at matched expert counts it outperforms token-choice routing on distribution shift benchmarks — suggesting that routing mechanism may matter more than routing structure (flat vs. hierarchical), and that the canonical token-choice framing is not the only or best flat routing design. The honest summary of the scaling evidence is that no published study directly pits flat-many-experts against hierarchical-few-experts-per-level at controlled compute and parameter budgets under distribution shift specifically — the field has optimized for average-case perplexity on training-adjacent distributions, and the distribution-shift axis remains a systematic blind spot in MoE scaling research.

The train-inference mismatch in expert choice routing is severe and largely unresolved in production: during training, each expert selects its top-k tokens from a batch of typically 4096–16384 tokens, meaning the selection threshold is implicitly set by the k-th highest affinity score across a large population — but at inference with a single token or small batch, there is no population to rank over, and the formulation collapses to either "every expert processes every token" (defeating sparsity entirely) or an arbitrary score threshold that was never trained. Zhou et al. (2022) acknowledged this directly and proposed falling back to token-choice routing at inference time, effectively training with one routing mechanism and deploying with another — this is not a minor implementation detail but a fundamental distributional shift baked into the architecture itself, where the router's learned affinities were shaped by expert-choice dynamics but are evaluated under token-choice dynamics at deployment. The practical consequence is that the load-balancing guarantee — the primary motivation for expert choice — exists only during training; at inference the routing reverts to the same potential collapse and imbalance problems as standard token-choice routing, but now with a router whose weights were optimized under a different selection pressure, making its token-choice behavior at inference potentially worse than a router trained end-to-end with token-choice. Some systems address this with hybrid routing schedules: training for the bulk of steps with expert choice to establish balanced specialization, then fine-tuning for a smaller number of steps with token-choice routing to adapt the router weights to the inference-time formulation — this is analogous to the exposure bias fix in sequence models (scheduled sampling, Bengio et al., 2015) but introduces a new hyperparameter (the switching step) with non-obvious optimal placement. No major open-source MoE serving framework (vLLM, DeepSpeed-MoE, Megablocks) implements expert-choice routing at inference as of mid-2025 — the operational complexity of the fallback plus the routing mismatch has made expert choice a training-time research result that has not crossed into production deployment, representing one of the larger gaps between MoE research findings and deployed MoE systems.
